summary: A 1971 description of the Initial Connection Protocol by A. M. McKenzie, a way for a user program to make its first connection to a service. It updates RFC 66 and RFC 80.

eli5.summary: The first handshake to get a conversation going with a service on another computer.

questions: how did early arpanet services get connected
what is server socket 1 in the icp
subtitle: A clarification to the Initial Connection Protocol: the 32-bit number is preceded by a data type code of zero.

tldr.problem: RFC 66 and RFC 80 defined the message from Server socket #1 as exactly an even 32 bit number, but it was unclear whether an eight-bit message data type code comes before it.
tldr.mechanism: The note observes that the only documented implementation, at UCSB, sends a code of zero, and that Steve Crocker indicated the Host-Host Protocol was intended to require the code.
tldr.outcome: It recommends amending RFC 66 and RFC 80 to show the 32 bit number is preceded by a message data type code of zero, the only code currently defined.

today: RFC 93 updates RFC 66 and RFC 80, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is a short 1971 clarification for an early ARPANET connection procedure.

sections.title: The Initial Connection Protocol
sections.content:
The Initial Connection Protocol (ICP) was first described in RFC 66 and restated in RFC 80. This note, by A. McKenzie of BBN, updates both after a review found an area of ambiguity.

The ambiguity also reflects one in the Host-Host Protocol Document No. 1.
sections.eli5: There is a standard way to say hello to a service on another computer. This note fixes one unclear sentence in the instructions for it.

sections.title: The Ambiguity
sections.content:
The unclear point is the message sent over the connection from Server socket #1. Both earlier RFCs define it as exactly an even 32 bit number. It was not clear whether this number follows an eight-bit message data type code, because the Host-Host Protocol makes provision for such codes but does not seem to absolutely demand them.

Only one implementation of an ICP had been documented in the NWG literature, the one at UCSB (RFC 74). Its implementers apparently read the Host-Host Protocol as demanding a message data type code, so they transmit a code of zero.
sections.eli5: The instructions said to send one number, but did not say whether a small label should come before it. The one team that had built it had added the label.

sections.title: The Recommended Amendment
sections.content:
Steve Crocker indicated in private communication that the Host-Host Protocol was intended to require a message data type code. On that basis the note recommends that RFC 66 and RFC 80 be amended so that the even 32 bit number is preceded by a message data type code of zero.

Zero is the only code currently defined, so the recommendation matches what the UCSB implementation already does.
sections.eli5: The answer is yes: put the label first, and the label is a zero. That is also what the one working version already did.
